Secretary of Defense
Pete Hegseth
discussed
Pentagon
business on at least 12 separate Signal app chats, the
Wall Street Journal
reported Monday, citing people familiar with his management practices.
Newsweek
reached out to the Pentagon for comment via email on Monday evening.
Why It Matters
The
Journal
's reporting indicates Hegseth used the encrypted messaging app far
more frequently than previously known
.
Trump administration officials' use of Signal came under scrutiny after
The Atlantic
reported earlier this year that Hegseth, then-national security adviser Mike Waltz and several other Cabinet-level officials discussed highly sensitive plans for a military strike against Yemen's Houthi militants in a Signal group chat that inadvertently included
The Atlantic
's editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg.
What To Know
In one instance, Hegseth directed his aides via Signal to notify foreign government officials about an ongoing military operation, the
Journal
reported. The defense secretary also used Signal to coordinate media appearance, plan foreign travel, manage his schedule and discuss other unclassified but sensitive issues, the report said.
The
Journal
reported that Hegseth set up many of the Signal chats himself and sent messages from an unsecured line at the Department of Defense, as well as from his personal phone.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, left, stands before the arrival of Peru's Foreign Affairs Minister Elmer Schialer and Peru's Minister of Defense Walter Astudillo at the Pentagon on May 5 in Washington.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, left, stands before the arrival of Peru's Foreign Affairs Minister Elmer Schialer and Peru's Minister of Defense Walter Astudillo at the Pentagon on May 5 in Washington.
Associated Press
The former
Fox News
host drew sharp backlash when Goldberg reported that he was mistakenly included in a Signal group chat in March where the defense secretary discussed extremely sensitive details about a military strike against Houthi targets in Yemen.
At the time, the strike had not yet been carried out and Hegseth included information about a specific target, the timing of the strike, weapons systems and precise attack sequencing, according to screenshots of the conversation that Goldberg published.
Goldberg reported that Waltz—who was
removed as national security adviser last week
—was the one who initially added him to the chat, which also included Vice President
JD Vance
, Secretary of State
Marco Rubio
,
CIA
Director
John Ratcliffe
, Director of National Intelligence
Tulsi Gabbard
and several other senior national security aides.
Hegseth has vehemently defended his reported conduct and he and the White House have insisted that no classified information was disclosed in that conversation or in others they've had using Signal.
Shortly after
The Atlantic
's story was published, it was also reported that Hegseth shared details about strikes in Yemen
in a second group chat
that included his wife and brother.
What People Are Saying
Marc Polymeropoulos, a former senior US intelligence officer, told the
Journal
:
"The use of personal phones and commercial apps introduces unnecessary risk. Signal is considered unclassified by the government for a reason. It's clear that U.S. government systems are having a hard time keeping up with the required pace of business."
Hegseth previously defended his use of Signal for sensitive discussions, writing on X:
"So, let's me get this straight. The Atlantic released the so-called 'war plans' and those 'plans' include: No names. No targets. No locations. No units. No routes. No sources. No methods. And no classified information. Those are some really s***** war plans. This only proves one thing: Jeff Goldberg has never seen a war plan or an 'attack plan' (as he now calls it). Not even close."
What Happens Next
The Pentagon's acting inspector general, Steve Stebbins, announced last month that he would investigate the defense secretary's use of Signal.
Reporting by the Associated Press contributed to this story.
